home.h1: AI writing tools that show their working
home.intro: Humanize, detect, paraphrase and proofread. Every result comes with what we actually measured, because a number with nothing behind it is not an answer.

humanize.metaTitle: Free AI humanizer — rewrite AI text to sound human
humanize.metaDescription: Rewrite generated text so it reads like a person wrote it, with the meaning intact. Three registers, free, no sign-up.
humanize.intro: Paste generated text and get its rhythm back: sentences of varied length, none of the usual filler, and the meaning untouched. Free, no account needed.

signals.description: Models write sentences of suspiciously similar length. This alternates long and short the way a person does.
"It is important to note", "in today's world", "plays a crucial role", "delve into". Gone.
Active voice, ordinary contractions and plain wording, instead of the register of an instruction manual.
Figures, names, quotations and technical terms stay exactly as they were. It adds no information and no opinions.

notes.title: Three registers, not one
notes.body: Academic uses the connectives of a university paper and an impersonal stance, without falling into the formulas that give a model away. Neutral is clear, direct prose that suits most writing. Informal is conversational without being sloppy. The register is chosen before you run it and genuinely changes the output, not just the tone of one sentence.

notes.title: What to expect, and what not to
notes.body: Humanizing is not a free pass through a detector. What it does is fix what actually gives generated text away: the flat cadence and the padding. If the original says little, it will still say little afterwards, and no rewriter fixes that. Nor is this for faking authorship: it is for making a generated draft sound like you before you rewrite it yourself.

faq.q: Does it change what my text means?
faq.a: It should not. The instruction is explicit: keep the meaning, the information and roughly the length. Figures, proper nouns, quotations and technical terms are kept verbatim. Read it before you hand it in anyway — no automatic rewrite is immune to shifting a nuance.

faq.q: Will it get past AI detectors?
faq.a: We do not promise that, and be wary of anyone who does. We fix the patterns detectors measure — flat rhythm, filler connectives, thin punctuation — which measurably lowers the signals. But detectors change, and guaranteeing a result on somebody else's tool would be selling you smoke.

faq.q: How many words can I process?
faq.a: Without an account, {anonWords} words a day and up to {anonRequest} per request. With a free account, {freeWords} a day. Paid plans raise both the monthly allowance and the size of a single request.

faq.q: Do you store my text?
faq.a: Only on paid plans, encrypted, so you have a history. On free plans the text is not stored at all: only the word count needed to apply the limits.

outro.lead: Want to check how much it reads as AI first?

detect.metaTitle: Free AI detector — evidence, not a percentage
detect.metaDescription: Check whether a text carries the traces of AI writing. You get the specific evidence, not an invented percentage. Free, no sign-up.
detect.intro: Paste a text and we tell you what we found: the rhythm of the sentences and the traces a copy-paste out of a chat leaves behind. No percentage, evidence in front of you. Free, no account needed.

signals.description: People alternate long and short sentences irregularly; models drift toward a flat cadence. It is the field's most robust finding and the one that best survives a rewrite.
Writing produces four-word sentences and forty-word sentences. Generated prose clusters between fifteen and twenty-five.
The spaced em dash, invisible characters, curly quotes, Markdown that survived the copy. Text typed by hand does not carry these.
Flawless spacing across two thousand words, without a single fossil correction, says something. We only count it in long texts, where it means anything.

notes.title: Why you will not see a percentage
notes.body: Tools advertising "92% AI-generated" have no way to stand behind that figure: there is no calibrated model that turns these signals into a real probability, and presenting one as though there were invites serious decisions on a fragile measurement. You get a band — no indications, some indications, clear indications — and underneath it the list of what we found, with examples. It is less impressive and it is more honest.

notes.title: The mistake we refuse to make
notes.body: This tool ends up pointed at students, and English AI detectors have a documented record of flagging people who did the work — non-native writers most of all, whose prose is measurably more regular. Missing generated text and accusing a person are not errors of equal cost, so the thresholds sit deliberately high, and the calibration corpus includes careful non-native English on purpose. If a change started flagging it, our test suite fails before the change ships.

notes.title: Under two hundred words we say nothing
notes.body: Variation measures need a sample. Below two hundred words or eight sentences the result would be noise wearing the costume of data, so we answer grey and tell you why. Paste residue is still reported at any length: an invisible character is an invisible character in twenty words as much as in two thousand.

faq.q: How does this AI detector work?
faq.a: It measures two things. The rhythm of the text: how much sentence length varies, how many sentences fall at the extremes, whether each sentence echoes the length of the last, how regular the paragraphs are. And the material traces of a copy-paste out of a chat: spaced em dashes, invisible characters, leftover Markdown, curly quotes. We score sliding windows of four sentences rather than the whole text, so a generated paragraph inside written work does not wash out in the average.

faq.q: Is it reliable? Can I use it to accuse someone?
faq.a: No. No AI detector, ours included, is evidence. They all produce false positives and false negatives: careful formal writing by a person can show indications, and generated text that was then rewritten by hand may show none. The result is orientation about style, never a verdict about authorship.

faq.q: Why no percentage, when everyone else gives one?
faq.a: Because it would be made up. "87% AI-generated" implies a statistical precision no current technique has. We give a qualitative band and, underneath, exactly what supports it, so you can look at the actual sentences and judge for yourself.

faq.q: Does it penalise non-native English?
faq.a: That is the failure mode we calibrate against. Second-language English tends to be more regular in rhythm, which is precisely what naive detectors read as machine-like. Careful non-native prose is part of the corpus the thresholds are set on, and it is pinned in the automated tests, so a change that starts flagging it breaks the build.

faq.q: How many words does it need?
faq.a: At least two hundred words and eight sentences. Below that we answer grey instead of handing you a meaningless number. You can analyse up to {anonWords} words a day without an account.

faq.q: Do you keep the texts I analyse?
faq.a: No. The analysis runs on our server against the text you send and is not stored: we only record the word count needed to apply your plan's limits.

outro.lead: Reads as AI and you want to fix it?

paraphrase.metaTitle: Paraphrasing tool — rewrite text in six registers
paraphrase.metaDescription: Rewrite any text in six registers while keeping what it says: standard, fluent, formal, simple, creative and academic.
paraphrase.intro: Rewrite a text in different words without losing what it says. Six registers, from academic to creative, with the changes marked so you can see what moved.

signals.description: A balanced rewrite: changes the wording without straying from the original. The sensible starting point.
Optimises for reading aloud. Unpicks heavy subordinate clauses and the sentences that make you stumble.
Impersonal stance, precise vocabulary and the connectives of a paper or a report. Academic also respects citation convention.
Simple drops the register until anyone can follow it. Creative allows imagery and turns the original did not have, with the same content.

notes.title: Paraphrasing is not swapping synonyms
notes.body: Replacing every word with a thesaurus entry produces text that reads strangely and, worse, keeps the same syntax: a marker spots it instantly and so does plagiarism software. What is needed is rebuilding the sentence. That is why the output may have a different number of sentences than the input, and why the changes are marked: so you review them rather than copy blind.

notes.title: About plagiarism
notes.body: Paraphrasing a source without citing it is still plagiarism, however well rewritten. This tool is for expressing what you have already understood and are going to attribute, not for dodging the attribution. If the text you start from is someone else's, you still need the citation.

faq.q: Does it keep the meaning?
faq.a: That is the stated goal, and figures, names and quotations are kept verbatim. In the creative register the distance from the original is greater by definition, so review that one more carefully than the rest.

faq.q: Will it help me avoid plagiarism?
faq.a: No. Paraphrasing a source without citing it is plagiarism either way. It helps you write in your own words something you are going to attribute properly.

faq.q: Is it included in the free plan?
faq.a: No. The paraphraser is on the paid plans. The humanizer and the detector do work without an account, at {anonWords} words a day.

faq.q: Can I see what changed?
faq.a: Yes. The result arrives with the differences marked against your original, so you review sentence by sentence instead of eyeballing two blocks of text.

outro.lead: Would you rather correct than rewrite?

correct.metaTitle: Grammar checker — spelling, grammar and punctuation
correct.metaDescription: Fix spelling, grammar, punctuation and agreement, with every change marked so you can review it.
correct.intro: Spelling, grammar, punctuation and agreement, with every change marked on your text. It fixes what is wrong without rewriting what is right.

signals.description: Including the pairs spellcheckers wave through because both words exist: their and there, its and it's, affect and effect.
Subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, dangling modifiers, preposition choice, pronoun reference.
Comma splices, missing serial commas where they change the meaning, unclosed quotes, apostrophes in plurals.
Your voice. It does not rewrite correct sentences for sport or shift your register: if it is right, it stays.

notes.title: Two modes, different ambition
notes.body: General mode fixes what is wrong and leaves the rest. Academic goes further: as well as correcting, it flags constructions that are valid but out of register — colloquialisms, verbal tics, overused passive voice — because in a university paper those cost marks too. If you only want the errors, stay in general.

notes.title: Why you see the differences
notes.body: A checker that hands back a clean block of text forces you to trust it blind or compare word by word. Here it arrives marked: every change shows against the original. It is more work to read and it is the only way to learn from the mistake instead of repeating it next month.

faq.q: British or American English?
faq.a: It follows whichever your text already uses rather than imposing one. What it will not do is leave a document half in one and half in the other, which is the error that actually looks careless.

faq.q: How is this different from my word processor's checker?
faq.a: A classic checker compares word by word against a dictionary and gets little right beyond spelling. This one reads the whole sentence, so it sees agreement, tense, preposition choice and punctuation, which is where nearly all real errors live.

faq.q: Is it included in the free plan?
faq.a: No. The grammar checker is on the paid plans. The humanizer and the detector work without an account.

faq.q: Will it change my style?
faq.a: In general mode, no: it corrects errors and leaves correct writing alone. In academic mode it does flag valid but out-of-register constructions, which is exactly what that mode is for.

outro.lead: Need to rephrase rather than correct?

sections.body: The company is established in the United States and your data is processed principally there, as well as on our providers' infrastructure. If you live outside the US, this involves an international transfer of data; the safeguards we apply are set out below.

sections.heading: What we process and why
sections.body: Account data (email address and, if you provide it, a name) to provide the service. Billing data, handled entirely by Stripe: we do not store card numbers. Usage metrics (word and request counts) to apply your plan's limits and detect abuse; IP addresses are always stored pseudonymised through a keyed hash, never in the clear. Product analytics with PostHog, which runs cookieless until you consent.

sections.heading: Your text
sections.body: Text from anonymous users and the free plan is not stored: we keep only the word count. To produce the result, the text is sent to our AI provider (Anthropic) through its API and is not used to train models. Document history is an optional feature of the paid plans and is stored encrypted with AES-256-GCM; you can turn it off or delete it whenever you like.

sections.heading: Providers
sections.body: We work with processors under contract: Supabase (database and authentication), Vercel (hosting), Stripe (payments), Anthropic (AI processing), Resend (transactional email), PostHog (analytics) and Sentry (error logging). We do not sell your personal data and do not share it with third parties for advertising.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: We keep your account data for as long as the account exists. When you delete your account we delete your personal data and your documents; we retain only billing records for the period required by US tax and accounting rules, and aggregate metrics that cannot identify you.

sections.heading: Your rights
sections.body: You can access, correct, export and delete your data. The quickest route is "My account", which includes deleting your account and your data. You can also write to {legalEmail}; we will respond within 30 days at most.

sections.heading: If you live in the EU, the EEA or the UK
sections.body: The GDPR applies to you. Our legal bases are: performance of the contract (account, providing the service, plan limits and billing), legitimate interest (security and abuse prevention) and your consent (cookie analytics and marketing communications). You have the rights of access, rectification, erasure, objection, restriction and portability, and to withdraw consent at any time. Transfers of data to the United States rely on the European Commission's standard contractual clauses signed with our providers. You may lodge a complaint with your country's supervisory authority — in Spain, the Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (aepd.es). To exercise any of these rights: {legalEmail}.

sections.heading: If you live in California
sections.body: The CCPA, as amended by the CPRA, applies to you. You have the right to know what categories of personal information we collect and why, to request its deletion, to correct it, to limit the use of sensitive personal information, and not to be treated differently for exercising these rights. We do not sell or share your personal information as the CCPA uses those terms, and that includes the information of anyone under 16. To exercise your rights: {legalEmail}.

sections.heading: Children
sections.body: The service is not directed at children under 13 and we do not knowingly collect their data. If we identify an account belonging to a child under 13, we delete it along with its data. If you believe a child in your care has given us data, write to us and we will resolve it.

sections.heading: Changes
sections.body: If we change this policy materially we will notify you by email or within the service before the change takes effect.

sections.heading: Cookies we use
sections.body: Strictly necessary technical cookies: the authentication session (Supabase) and interface preferences. Without them the service cannot work. Analytics (PostHog): runs in cookieless mode until you consent through the banner; if you consent, analytics cookies are used. Advertising (Google): only with your consent, through Consent Mode v2.

sections.heading: Managing your consent
sections.body: You can accept, reject or change your choice at any time from the cookie banner or from your browser settings. Rejecting analytics and advertising does not affect how the service works or your plan's limits.

sections.heading: We do not sell or share your information
sections.body: We do not use cookies to sell or share personal information for cross-context behavioural advertising, as the CCPA uses those terms. If you live in California and want to exercise your rights, write to {legalEmail}.

legal.jurisdiction: a limited liability company organised in the State of Florida, United States

raya_espaciada.label: Spaced em dash
raya_espaciada.explanation: {count, plural, one {One em dash (—) with a space} other {# em dashes (—) with spaces}} on either side, at {per1000} per 1,000 words. British style allows this, so on its own it proves nothing — but it is also the dash a chat interface produces, and it is not on most keyboards.

caracteres_invisibles.label: Invisible characters
caracteres_invisibles.explanation: {count, plural, one {One invisible character} other {# invisible characters}} (zero-width space or similar). Nobody types these: they arrive when text is copied out of a web interface.

homoglifos.label: Letters from another alphabet
homoglifos.explanation: {count, plural, one {One word mixes} other {# words mix}} Latin letters with Cyrillic or Greek. This is not evidence of machine writing: it is evidence that the text has been through an evasion tool.

markdown_superviviente.label: Leftover Markdown
markdown_superviviente.explanation: {count, plural, one {One piece} other {# pieces}} of unconverted Markdown: asterisk bold, hash headings or rules. These survive a copy out of a chat.

comillas_curvas.label: Curly quotation marks
comillas_curvas.explanation: {count, plural, one {One curly quotation mark} other {# curly quotation marks}} in an otherwise plain text. A word processor produces these too, so they count for little on their own.

emojis_estructurales.label: Emoji used as bullets
emojis_estructurales.explanation: {count, plural, one {One line starts} other {# lines start}} with an emoji in a bullet position, a very characteristic layout pattern.

espacios_especiales.label: Special spaces
espacios_especiales.explanation: {count, plural, one {One special space} other {# special spaces}} (non-breaking or thin) instead of an ordinary one.

semirraya_como_raya.label: En dash used as a dash
semirraya_como_raya.explanation: {count, plural, one {One en dash (–) used} other {# en dashes (–) used}} where a dash goes. Standard in British style, so this counts for little by itself.

puntos_suspensivos_unicode.label: Single-character ellipsis
puntos_suspensivos_unicode.explanation: The ellipsis appears as one character (…) rather than three full stops, {count, plural, one {once} other {# times}}. Word autocorrect does this as well.

apostrofo_tipografico.label: Curly apostrophe
apostrofo_tipografico.explanation: {count, plural, one {One curly apostrophe} other {# curly apostrophes}} (’) rather than the straight one. Every word processor produces these, so this barely counts in English.

vinetas_uniformes.label: Uniform bullets
vinetas_uniformes.explanation: {count, plural, one {One bullet} other {# bullets}} in identical format.

listas_numeradas_perfectas.label: Numbered list with no gaps
listas_numeradas_perfectas.explanation: {count} consecutive numbered list items, with no gaps and no restarts.

encabezado_negrita_dos_puntos.label: Bold headings with colons
encabezado_negrita_dos_puntos.explanation: {count, plural, one {One paragraph starts} other {# paragraphs start}} with a bold heading followed by a colon.

apertura_interrogacion_perfecta.label: Opening marks never dropped
apertura_interrogacion_perfecta.explanation: Every question and exclamation carries its opening mark.

espaciado_impecable.label: Spacing without a single slip
espaciado_impecable.explanation: Across {words} words there is not one double space and not one space before a punctuation mark.

ausencia_correcciones_fosiles.label: Not one fossil correction
ausencia_correcciones_fosiles.explanation: No word accidentally repeated and no sentence abandoned half-written, which is what usually survives when someone writes straight through.

cv_longitud_frase.label: Sentence length variation
cv_longitud_frase.explanation: Sentence lengths vary with a coefficient of {value}. Native English prose usually sits between 0.45 and 0.70; below 0.30 the rhythm is flat. Careful second-language writing also sits low, which is why this alone does not move the band. Mean of {meanWords} words per sentence.

distribucion_longitudes.label: Very short and very long sentences
distribucion_longitudes.explanation: A proportion of {value} of the sentences is very short (five words or fewer) or very long (thirty-five or more). Writing produces both extremes; generated prose clusters in the middle.

autocorrelacion_longitudes.label: Length echoing
autocorrelacion_longitudes.explanation: Each sentence echoes the length of the one before it with a correlation of {value}. The higher it runs, the more metronomic the rhythm.

varianza_longitud_palabra.label: Word length variation
varianza_longitud_palabra.explanation: Word lengths vary with a coefficient of {value}.

varianza_densidad_silabica.label: Syllable variation
varianza_densidad_silabica.explanation: Syllables per word vary with a coefficient of {value}.

uniformidad_parrafos.label: Paragraph regularity
uniformidad_parrafos.explanation: The paragraphs run to {shape} sentences: a variation of {value}. Generated writing produces paragraphs of three or four sentences with almost metrical regularity.
